title: Bring the zsh prompt's chips in line with the label-chip definition
description:
docs/lcars-design.md was rewritten on 2026-09-22: the hole chip and notch chip styles are merged into one LABEL chip (the bar's accent as TEXT, cut into black), 'notch' now means the one-column vertical highlight before a cap, Style A/B are gone, and placement is cap-side rather than rightmost. The dashboard follows that; the zsh prompt does not.

WHAT IS WRONG. zsh/prompt_lcars.zsh's header comment still defines 'chip = labeled segment (Style B), notch = accent text on black (Style A)'. The cwd chip is still drawn the old hole way -- dark text on the bar's colour with no fill change -- where the new definition makes it a label chip: accent text on black, with at least one column of black padding each side.

WHY IT MATTERS. The cwd is the prompt's own title, the same role the dashboard's panel titles play, so it should read the same way. Two surfaces drawing the same element two ways is the drift docs/lcars-design.md exists to prevent.

SCOPE. The prompt's own comments and whatever draws the chip. Placement is already cap-side there (the cap is at the right and the elbow at the left), so this is colour and padding, not layout.

title: Live data widgets: active Jira tickets and GitHub PR queue
description: Two usefulness panes on the dashboard: assigned Jira work items that are not Done, and the user's open pull requests plus PRs awaiting their review. Data access must degrade gracefully — the pane renders with a stale/offline marker rather than breaking the layout when a source is unreachable or unauthenticated.
notes:
JIRA ACCESS IS THE ONE UNRESOLVED PIECE. acli is installed at /opt/homebrew/bin/acli but NOT authenticated ('unauthorized: use acli jira auth login'), and login is interactive so an agent cannot complete it. Seth runs one command to turn the live path on:

    acli jira auth login

Until then the pane reads a cache at ~/.cache/lcarcat/dashboard/jira-work-items.json, which is currently populated with 50 real work items (13 in flight, 2 blocked) pulled via the Atlassian MCP server on 2026-09-11. The pane shows a CACHED-<age> chip so stale data is never mistaken for live. dashboard/tools/refresh_jira_cache.py refills it from any JQL search result — REST, MCP, or a bare list.

GitHub needed no such workaround: gh owns auth and already works. Used ONE gh api graphql call rather than two 'gh search prs' calls because the REST search gh exposes via --json cannot return reviewDecision or statusCheckRollup, and those two fields are what decide whether a PR needs attention. Verified live: 10 authored, 10 awaiting review.

BUG FOUND AND FIXED during this work: the Jira cache round-trip silently dropped issue_type and status_category, because the cache is written from the dataclass (whose field names differ from Jira's) and parse_item only read Jira's spelling. Symptom was 13 active items live vs 11 after reload. Pinned by test_cache_round_trip_preserves_every_field.
close_reason: Both panes render real data. Jira is on the cache path pending one interactive acli login; GitHub is fully live.

title: Dashboard widget protocol + layout presets
description: A widget renders into a Rect on the shared canvas and knows nothing about its neighbours. Layouts are named presets composing widgets into panel grids, so several dashboard variations exist without duplicating render code.

title: LCARS dashboard: canvas + reusable segment library
description: Foundation for the 2cc demo page: an absolute-positioned cell canvas that paints one ANSI frame, plus reusable LCARS segment primitives (bar, elbow, stem, cap, chip, notch, pill, meter, panel) built on the repo's cells-for-flat/PNG-for-curves rule. Segments must be usable by any widget without knowing about it.
design:
Canvas + segments landed. Key decisions:

ABSOLUTE POSITIONING, ONE WRITE PER FRAME. The canvas is a cell grid serialised once, not printed line by line. Two reasons: a dashboard painted pane-by-pane tears visibly, and kitty image escapes MUST reach the terminal before the placeholder cells referencing them — batching both into one string makes that ordering a property of the string rather than of terminal read scheduling.

PANEL IS THE UNIT WIDGETS MEET. Panel.draw() paints chrome and returns the content Rect. No widget computes a chrome offset, so a layout can change a panel's style without editing any widget. The OUTER FRAME IS ALSO A PANEL — there is no separate frame concept, which is what keeps elbow/rail/cap rules identical at both nesting levels.

FULL DIACRITIC TABLE. zsh/prompt_lcars.zsh hardcodes only the first 5 row/column diacritics because its widest image is a 5-col elbow. dashboard/diacritics.py transcribes all 297 from kitty's shipped table, so panel images are not capped at 5 cells. Transcribed rather than read at runtime: kitty ships it at a path containing a content hash that changes between releases.
close_reason: Canvas, geometry, assets, images and the segment library are in place and exercised by 42 unit tests plus four rendered layouts.

title: kitty SIGBUS: non-atomic PNG writes truncate assets kitty has mmap'd
description:
kitty 0.48.2 crashed 2026-08-26 16:52 EDT with SIGBUS while decoding one of our PNGs.
Crash report: kitty-crash-report-2026-08-1600EDT.txt (repo root, untracked).

EVIDENCE
  Exception:  EXC_BAD_ACCESS (SIGBUS), KERN_MEMORY_ERROR at 0x1186bc029
  Region:     "mapped file" 1186bc000-1186c0000 [16K] r--/r-- (fault 41 bytes in)
  Triage:     CL   - cluster_pagein past EOF
              APFS - cluster_pagein() failed
              VM   - Filesystem pagein returned an error in vnode_pagein
  Stack:      main thread -> kitty.fast_data_types -> png_read_image ->
              png_read_row -> _platform_memmove  (crash frame)

"cluster_pagein past EOF" with a fault only 41 bytes into the mapping means the
file got SHORTER than the mapping while libpng was reading rows out of it - i.e.
truncated to ~0 underneath kitty. Not a decode bug, not bad PNG data.

MECHANISM
1. zsh/prompt_lcars.zsh:114-122 (_lc_transmit) transmits with t=f - kitty is
   handed a PATH (base64'd) and reads/mmaps the file ASYNCHRONOUSLY, on its own
   schedule. The function's own comment says so. Paths point at
   _LCARS_DIR (line 14), the deployed kitty/lcars asset directory.
2. deploy.sh:70 copies into that exact directory with a plain in-place copy,
   which opens the destination O_TRUNC: the file is 0 bytes for the duration of
   the copy. AGENTS.md tells us to run ./deploy.sh after EVERY edit.
3. generate/gen_swoops.py:144,166,205 call img.save(path) - PIL also truncates
   in place. Same hazard for the nvim cache asset dir, whose files
   image_registry hands to image.nvim by path.

So: deploy (or regenerate assets) while any kitty window is drawing an LCARS
prompt, and kitty can be mid-png_read_image on a file just truncated under it.

TIMING: commits at 15:05 and 15:16 that afternoon, crash at 16:52 - an active
dev session. mtimes on the deployed 19x38 PNGs were overwritten by later
deploy.sh runs (2026-08-27 10:48), so mtime evidence is gone, but the nvim cache
dir shows no write in the crash window, which rules that path out and leaves the
deployed dir as the exposed one.

FIX OPTIONS (not mutually exclusive)
 A. Atomic writes - write a sibling temp file, then rename(2) (atomic on APFS).
    A rename swaps the directory entry; kitty's existing mapping keeps the old
    inode alive until it closes it, so there is never a window where the mapped
    file is short.
      deploy.sh:70   copy to "$dest.tmp.$$", then mv -f onto "$dest"
      gen_swoops.py  img.save(tmp); os.replace(tmp, path)   x3 sites
    This is the general fix - it also covers the nvim/image.nvim consumer.
 B. Switch _lc_transmit to t=d (inline base64 PNG bytes). kitty never opens the
    file, so there is nothing to race. The comment above the printf already
    describes t=d as the synchronous, race-free choice - it reads as if the code
    once did this and regressed to t=f. Also fixes the "can miss the first
    placeholder draw" problem the same comment describes.

NOTE: that comment and the code disagree today (comment explains t=d; the printf
sends t=f). Worth resolving either way.
notes:
Option A (atomic writes) implemented 2026-08-27. Option B (t=d vs t=f in
_lc_transmit) deliberately NOT done — still open on this bead.

CHANGES
  deploy.sh deploy_one()      copy to "$dest.deploy.$$", cmp the temp, then
                              mv -f onto the destination. All three steps
                              guarded; on any failure the temp is removed and
                              the destination is left untouched.
  gen_swoops.py save_atomic() new helper; the 3 img.save(path) sites now call
                              it. Temp keeps a .png suffix because PIL infers
                              the format from the extension.
  docs/asset-pipeline.md      new "Never rewrite an asset PNG in place" section
                              stating the invariant and why.

VERIFICATION
  - Patched generator vs the pre-patch generator (extracted from git HEAD),
    same args: output byte-for-byte identical. The change is behavior-preserving.
  - 17 assets generated, zero leftover *.tmp.png.
  - deploy.sh: 33 files ok, no FAIL/SKIP, zero leftover *.deploy.* temps.
  - Atomicity proven by inode: destination inode changed across a deploy
    (37499691 -> 37499885), i.e. the file was replaced by rename, not written
    in place. An existing mmap therefore keeps the old inode.
  - Failure path exercised against a read-only destination dir: prints FAIL,
    returns 1, leaves the old destination content intact, no temp left behind.
    (Strictly better than before — the old cp would have left the destination
    truncated.)
  - Runtime cache-miss path checked too: chrome.lua:27 and the zsh prompt shell
    out to the DEPLOYED gen_swoops.py copy; that copy has save_atomic and
    regenerates correctly.

INCIDENTAL FINDING (not addressed, not a regression)
  Regenerating the 19x38 periwinkle set reproduces 11 of the committed
  assets/*.png with identical PIXELS but different bytes — Pillow/zlib version
  drift in the encoder, pre-existing. Only matters if byte-comparing assets.
close_reason: Both fix options landed. A (atomic writes: deploy.sh temp+rename, gen_swoops os.replace) in 7f88706; B (t=d inline transmission, plus chunking) in e9c8de3. The t=f/t=d comment-vs-code contradiction the bead flagged is resolved — code, function comment and docs/kitty-graphics.md now agree. Not a regression: t=f dated from the initial commit, so the prose described an intent never implemented. Verified by byte-identical payload round-trip on both single and chunked paths, and live kitty captures of the elbow/cap plus font-resize retransmission.

title: Tab A right cap hidden by bar highlight extmark
description:
Regression introduced by the 2m7.10 attempted fix for right-cap sharp corners. In `nvim/lua/lcars/block_demo.lua:321`, `bar_w = (lp + bw) - bar_x0` extends the LcarsBlockBar extmark across cap_x..cap_x+1 (the two cells where the vcap image sits). The extmark renders at HL_PRI=200 which sits above the image in nvim + image.nvim + kitty, so a solid periwinkle rectangle covers the cap entirely.

## Observed
User: "The caps at the ends of headers and footers is missing, probably a BG color overlay extending past the caps. If I scroll the viewport right, since the caps are fixed position on scroll, I can see them." (Scrolling separates screen-coord images from buffer-coord extmarks — confirms the cause.)

## Affects
All four barrow calls in make_A: header rows h0, h0+1 and footer rows f0+1, f0+2 (block_demo.lua:324-330).

## Constraint
The reverse fix (`bar_w = cap_x - bar_x0`) restores cap visibility but reopens the original 2b "sharp corner" problem: the vcap PNG has transparent outer corners, so with bar highlight stopping at cap_x, those pixels reveal LcarsBlockBg (black) as square notches instead of a smooth round terminus.

## Constraints for the real fix
- Must not paint a solid highlight over the cap image at higher priority than the image.
- Must produce a rounded terminus (no black square corners).
- Must survive viewport scroll (i.e., not depend on the cap's screen position matching an extmark's buffer position — that fails under scroll anyway, and is what caused this regression to be visible).

## Possible directions (do not lock in — see AGENTS.md, no prescriptive fixes)
- Bake periwinkle into the cap PNG's outer-corner pixels so no cell needs a background behind them.
- Paint a 2-cell periwinkle extmark on the cap cells at a lower priority than the image, if image.nvim exposes a way to render images above extmarks (needs verification).
- Confirm whether the "sharp corner" 2b was ever visible on Tab A before this session, or whether it only appeared in a specific screenshot scale — the original observation may have been marginal.

## Verification for close
- Cap visible on Tab A header (block 1, rows 1-2) and footer (block 1, rows 17-18) without scrolling.
- No black square corners at the cap's outer edges.
- Regression check: scroll viewport right by 20 cols, caps still align with the elbow structure.
close_reason: Fixed via bar_w = cap_x - bar_x0 in nvim/lua/lcars/block_demo.lua make_A. Bar highlight now stops one cell short of the 2-cell vcap so both cap cells fall back to LcarsBlockBg (black), letting the vcap PNG's semicircle render intact (periwinkle interior, transparent outer corners over black). Verified pixel-precise on all 6 caps (3 blocks × header+footer) at narrow (bw=32) and full window widths. Sign-off received.

title: (EPIC) LCARS kitty tab bar: design feedback, features, bugs
description:
Standing home for the custom kitty tab bar — Seth's design feedback, feature ideas, and bug reports as it gets daily use.

WHAT EXISTS. kitty/tab_bar.py, loaded by 'tab_bar_style custom' in kitty/lcars.conf, deployed to ~/.config/kitty/tab_bar.py. It draws the whole strip rather than filling in a per-tab title template, because a template describes ONE tab and cannot produce a left rail stub or a right-aligned readout.

Current layout, left to right: a 2-column orange rail stub; one capped pill per tab carrying an LCARS-form 'NN-NAME' title, orange when active and periwinkle when not, separated by single black columns; then right-aligned, a gold stardate pill and a sky-blue clock pill.

One-row bar rules apply: flat runs are colored cells, the rounded ends are the powerline half-circle glyphs (the kitty graphics protocol is not available on that strip), and tab backgrounds stay black in lcars.conf so the caps render on black — a cap over a colored background fills its own notch and squares the corner.

REVERTING. If tab_bar.py ever raises, the tab bar disappears in every kitty window at once. Recovery is one line: set 'tab_bar_style powerline' in ~/.config/kitty/lcars.conf:64 and reload. The two original title templates are still there, commented, directly below it.

TESTING. test/captures/tab_bar.sh builds an ISOLATED kitty config directory from the repo and shoots one, two and three tabs. Do not test by deploying first — that is how you take down the tab bar in the window you are working in.
design:
Open questions, none of them settled, all worth Seth's opinion.

RIGHT-HAND READOUT. Currently stardate + clock. That real estate could carry anything: host name, git branch, battery, the Jira/PR counts the dashboard already fetches, a red-alert indicator. It is the most valuable and least considered part of the strip.

TITLE REWRITING. _lcars_title takes the last path segment, uppercases it, and prefixes a two-digit index. That is lossy in a way that may or may not matter: a shell and an nvim in the same directory produce identical pills. kitty knows the running process; using it would distinguish them.

ACTIVITY AND BELLS. kitty can report that a background tab has activity or rang a bell. Nothing in the strip shows it. The LCARS answer is probably a color change rather than a glyph, since the palette already carries red-alert.

MANY TABS. Titles truncate with an ellipsis and the group is clipped to leave room for the readout, but this has only been seen at one, two and three tabs. Behaviour at ten is unknown, and 'drop whole pills rather than clip one' may be the better rule — it is what draw_chips settled on for the dashboard.

CLICK TO SWITCH. kitty handles tab clicks itself, but whether a fully custom draw_tab preserves the hit regions has not been checked. Worth confirming before assuming it works.

BLOCK LETTERING. lcarcat-6ac wants Impact/condensed block letters across two surfaces and names the tab bar as one of them. On that strip the graphics protocol is unavailable, so the only route is a PUA-remapped font — which is exactly what 6ac already proposes. Related, not duplicate.

VISUAL CONTINUITY. The rail stub is two orange columns at the far left. Whether it should align with, or hand off to, the dashboard's own left rail below it is an open composition question.
acceptance_criteria: Seth has used it daily and the feedback here is either addressed or consciously deferred.
notes:
A running kitty caches the tab_bar module, so 'ctrl+a>f' (load_config_file) does NOT reliably pick up a changed tab_bar.py — kitty has to be restarted. That is a real cost during iteration and worth knowing before chasing a change that appears not to have applied.

Deployed and verified byte-identical to the repo on 2026-09-16. Rendering was checked in an isolated config at one, two and three tabs: rounded caps flush with the pill bodies, correct active/inactive colours, right-aligned readout holding position regardless of tab count. Not yet used in anger.
IMAGES IN THE STRIP: not possible with stock kitty (0.48.2). Verified 2026-09-16 by source reading and a live spike: the tab bar Screen has window_id 0 and graphics.c upload_to_gpu() bails out when window_id is 0, so the image is accepted and placed but never uploaded. Caps stay as powerline glyphs; the block-lettering route stays the PUA font of lcarcat-6ac. Full write-up: docs/kitty-tab-bar.md.
UPSTREAM SEARCH (2026-09-16): no kitty issue or discussion asks for graphics-protocol images in the tab bar (searched issues + Discussions; #4447 'Share your tab bar style' is all glyph/colour work). The window_id guard in graphics.c upload_to_gpu is not a tab-bar decision: it has been there since before 354d7c2 (2021-01-31, a restructure of an existing 'if (self->window_id && ...)'), and exists because a GraphicsManager with no window has no GL context to make current. The tab bar Screen is still Screen(None, 1, 10, 0, ...) on master. So: unrequested and incidental, not designed against.

RELOAD, EXPLAINED FROM SOURCE (not yet tested live): kitty >= 0.45 (83f0d6b, discussion #9221) makes load_config_file clear the cached tab_bar.py module — but boss.load_config_file calls apply_new_options() (which re-reads the cached draw_tab into TabBar.draw_func) BEFORE tab_bar.clear_caches(). So the first ctrl+a>f keeps the old draw_tab and a SECOND ctrl+a>f should pick up the edit. That is the 'does not reliably reload' observed above, and a one-line ordering bug worth reporting upstream. Written up in docs/kitty-tab-bar.md.
RELOAD CONFIRMED LIVE (2026-09-17, kitty 0.48.2): marker-logging draw_tab + two 'kitty @ load-config' runs: VERSION-1 after the first reload, VERSION-2 only after the second. Fix drafted on branch fix-tab-bar-reload-order in ~/code/kitty (move tab_bar.clear_caches() ahead of apply_new_options()).

title: Elbow corner radius is too tight; derive the right ratio from canon references
description:
The dashboard's elbows read as far tighter than real LCARS. Seth flagged it against the holodeck and Voyager PADD references and then added four production-prop images under references/canon/ to measure properly.

Two separate problems.

GEOMETRY. gen_swoops.make_swoop computes the outer and inner radii independently: r_out = min(cell_height*0.9, bar_height), r_in = min(stem_width*0.9, cell_height*0.6). For the standard 2-row bar that puts the two arc centres 235px apart, and the outer radius at 0.45x the bar thickness. Whatever the correct ratio turns out to be, radii derived independently cannot express a consistent corner.

RATIO. Unknown. That is what this bead is for.
design:
A candidate rule came up and is worth recording with its status.

R_inner = R_outer - W, where W is the thickness of the bar making the turn. Seth found this stated as guidance but could not find a citation, so treat it as unverified.

What IS certain, because it is forced geometry rather than a claim: two arcs cannot share a centre AND each be tangent to its own edge unless the two arms have equal width. So 'concentric' is wrong whenever the thick-to-thin rule applies, which is always. The defensible reading of the rule is that the two centres share a HEIGHT (for a top-left elbow) and differ horizontally by stem_width - bar_thickness. That is algebraically equivalent to R_inner = R_outer - W.

Consequence worth knowing before choosing a ratio: R_outer must exceed the bar thickness or R_inner goes negative. At today's 0.45x it computes to -167px. The current elbow is not merely tight, it is a shape the construction cannot produce, which is why the code derives the radii independently.

Cost: a valid elbow needs a bigger asset. Roughly 6x4 cells at 1.25x, 7x4 at 1.5x, 8x5 at 1.78x, against 5x3 today. Those rows come out of every panel's content area, so the ratio is a layout decision, not only a drawing one.

An interactive study of the construction was published as an artifact:
https://claude.ai/code/artifact/74a699e1-4983-48d9-bd60-7ede82f29d7a
acceptance_criteria: Elbow radius ratio chosen and justified by measurements of named corners in references/canon/. gen_swoops derives the inner radius from the outer rather than independently. Panel learns the elbow's real cell size instead of assuming 5x3. Layouts still fit at 80x24.
notes:
MEASUREMENT IS THE HARD PART. Three automated attempts failed; do not repeat them.

1. Sliding-window circle fits along traced contours. Returned every radius as ~48-53px across images from 400px to 1920px wide. The tell was that the result had no relationship to image scale: it was fitting circles to the staircase of compressed edges, not to arcs.

2. Corner-inset on quantised flat-colour regions. Fixed the scaling, but with no minimum arm size and no way to tell an L-shaped elbow from a rounded rectangle it returned ratios from 0.68 to 14.17, the outliers all sitting on 3-5px 'bars'.

3. Same, plus an L-shape test (fill fraction 0.22-0.80 of the bounding box) and a 7px minimum arm. Produced a tight-looking median of 0.77 across 11 detections -- but Seth reviewed the annotated output and confirmed it was not measuring actual elbows in three of the four images. The number is void. Note 0.77 was self-evidently suspect anyway: below 1.0 it makes R_inner negative, the same failure as the current code.

An earlier hand-picked measurement of ONE elbow in the Voyager PADD image gave R_outer/W = 1.78, with both arcs fitting circles at 0.23px rms. That single figure is the only measurement not known to be wrong, but n=1 and it should not be generalised.

WHAT WORKS: measuring a corner whose location is known. Fitting circles to a hand-picked boundary gave a clean sub-pixel residual. The failure is always detection, never measurement.

SUGGESTED NEXT STEP: have Seth name the elbows. Grid overlays at 100px cells were generated for all four references and sent; naming a handful of cells per image is enough to drive a targeted measurement. Do not build a fourth heuristic detector.

The scratch tool test/fixtures/measure_elbows.py was deleted rather than left in the tree, because it produces confident wrong numbers and someone would run it and believe them.

references/canon/ is currently UNTRACKED. The repo's .gitignore already excludes two similar reference images at the root, so committing prop screen-grabs may be deliberate policy; Seth should decide before this bead is picked up, since the measurement depends on those files.
MEASURED 2026-09-17 from Seth's hand crops in references/elbows/ (tool: scratch measure.py; the crops are transformed to a top-left elbow, the straight edges come from stable far-end profiles, and each corner gets a circle fit constrained tangent to both edges, cross-checked by a free circle fit and an ellipse fit; every overlay was visually verified).
Valid elbows (px, thick arm / thin arm / R_outer / r_inner):
- msd-2 (TNG Generations): stem 22.4 / bar 7.3 / R 20.3 (ellipse 18.9x21.7) / r 17.2 (15.8-19.8). R/thin 2.8, R/thick 0.91, r/thin 2.4.
- voyager PADD (fan recreation by cmdrkerner): stem 58.9 / bar 9.9 / R 29.2 (all fits agree, rms 0.07) / r 13.9 (free fit 16.3). R/thin 2.9, R/thick 0.50, r/thin 1.4-1.6.
- msd-1 (TNG Generations): stem 148.9 / bar 27.5 / outer NOT circular: best ellipse 85.5 along the bar x 56.6 along the stem (rms 0.8), best circle 69 (rms 1.8) / r 26.2 (free 19.5). R/thin 2.1-3.1, R/thick 0.38-0.57.
- holodeck top-left and top-right (provenance unknown): here the HORIZONTAL arm is thicker: bar 29.4 / stem 22.5-23.2 / R 22.9-24.1 / r 19.2-19.4. R/thin 1.03, R/thick 0.8, r/thin 0.85.
Invalid: the holodeck crop's two bottom junctions are square (the stems meet a 10px bar at right angles, with no radius at all).
FINDINGS: (1) R_outer lies between the thin and thick arm widths in every case. (2) With thick/thin >= 3 (the three stem-heavy elbows), R_outer = 2.5-3x the thin arm and 0.4-0.9x the thick arm. (3) r_inner = R_outer - W does NOT hold with either arm as W: msd-2 predicts 13.0 vs 17.2, voyager 19.3 vs 13.9, holodeck 0.7 vs 19.3. The rule should be dropped. (4) The concentric / same-height centre rule also fails (vertical centre offsets +4, -5, +25 px).
DASHBOARD CONTEXT: our thick arm is the horizontal bar (2 rows = 76px) and the thin arm is the stem (1 col = 19px), thick/thin = 4, i.e. the canon proportions rotated. Today R_out = 34px (1.8x thin, 0.45x thick) and r_in = 17px (0.9x thin). Applying the canon ratios gives R_out of about 48-57px and r_in of about 27-45px. R_out 57 with r_in 38 still fits the current 5x3 asset (95x114px). Whether canon ratios transfer to the rotated proportions is Seth's call.
RECONCILED WITH THE EARLIER STUDY (artifact FQTrtUvd19xQpLeBBnpTVK) 2026-09-17. The arc fits agree: that study had outer R 28.5 / inner 14.9 / centre offsets (44, -4.2) for the Voyager elbow; this session measured 29.2 / 13.9 / (43.6, -5.4) on the same corner. The disagreement is entirely W. The study never measured the bar: it inferred W=16 from the rule it was testing (dx = stem - bar, so 58.9 - 44 = 14.9 ~ 16). Measured directly the bar is 9.9px, which turns 'R_outer = 1.78 x W' into 2.9 x W and makes the whole 'today is 4x too tight' framing wrong. R/thick for our elbow is 0.45, inside the measured canon range of 0.37-0.91.
NO FORMULA. Least squares over the five elbows: R = 0.72*thin + 0.26*thick is the best two-term fit and still misses by 45% at worst; every single-term fit is worse (R = 1.54*thin, 52% worst; R = 0.42*thick, 54%). The tightest one-parameter law is R_outer ~ sqrt(thin*thick) (0.86-1.59x, within +-17% once the tiny low-res msd-2 elbow is set aside). n=5 from four images, two sharing one image, so none of this is a law.
HEURISTIC THAT DOES HOLD (all five elbows): (1) thin <= R_outer <= thick, i.e. the outer radius always lands between the two arm widths; (2) R_inner = 0.48-0.85 x R_outer; (3) R_inner >= ~0.8 x thin arm, never a token notch; (4) both arcs are circles tangent to their own two edges (msd-1's outer is an ellipse at 1.5:1, so a sweep need not be circular); (5) the turn never pinches - the narrowest colour across the corner equals the thin arm (0.91-1.02x). Square-cornered junctions like the holodeck footers are a different element, not a broken elbow.
DISPROVED, DO NOT REINSTATE: R_inner = R_outer - W (fails 4/5, up to 18px) and centres-share-a-height (vertical offsets -15, +4, -5, +25, +26). Because the arcs are independent, R_outer need not exceed either arm and there is no negative-inner-radius failure mode.
OUR ELBOW: thin arm 19px (1-col stem), thick arm 76px (2-row bar). Today R_outer 34 (1.8x thin, 0.45x thick) and R_inner 17 (0.9x thin, 0.5x R) - both already inside the measured bounds. sqrt(thin*thick) = 38. The canon-like end of the range is R_outer 38-55 with R_inner 24-38, which still fits the 5x3 asset (95x114px). So the acceptance criterion 'derive the right ratio' resolves to a range, and what is left to decide is where in it to sit and whether gen_swoops should derive R_inner from R_outer as a fraction (0.5-0.85) rather than independently.
DECIDED 2026-09-22 (Seth, from the elbow tuner artifact HFUgykZAmofEPaEhZTZnyH): R_outer = 1.0 x the thick arm's width, R_inner = 0.48 x R_outer, outer sweep always circular. For the dashboard elbow that is R_outer 76px (was 34) and R_inner 36.5px (was 17); the fillet ends at 112.5px in a 114px image, so the 5x3 asset is unchanged and no layout loses rows. Implemented in generate/gen_swoops.py as ELBOW_OUTER_RADIUS_OVER_THICK_ARM and ELBOW_INNER_OVER_OUTER_RADIUS, both tunable; make_swoop now derives the inner radius from the outer instead of computing the two independently. The eight checked-in periwinkle assets were regenerated. Note for the record: 1.0x the thick arm is a shade past the measured maximum (0.91x) and 0.48 is the bottom of the measured inner band, so this is a deliberate look rather than the centre of the references.
close_reason: Radius settled and shipped. Measured five elbows across four reference props (arcs and arms, arms along their full length in the full-size sources); they support bounds, not a formula, and both previously recorded rules (R_inner = R_outer - W, and shared centre height) are disproved and marked as such in docs/lcars-design.md. Seth chose R_outer = the thick arm's width and R_inner = 0.48 x R_outer, always circular: 76px and 36.5px for the dashboard elbow, against 34 and 17. gen_swoops.make_swoop now derives the inner radius from the outer via ELBOW_OUTER_RADIUS_OVER_THICK_ARM and ELBOW_INNER_OVER_OUTER_RADIUS (both tunable); assets regenerated and deployed, with deploy.sh --prune-assets added because asset filenames do not encode geometry. Acceptance: ratio chosen and justified - yes; inner derived from outer - yes; 'panel learns the elbow's real cell size' - moot, the asset stayed 5x3 (95x114) because the fillet ends at 112.5px, so no panel lost a row; layouts at 80x24 - verified, all five layouts render at 80x24, 120x40 and 181x57, with images on and off, and the dashboard's own cache regenerated at the new geometry. Method and traps written up in docs/elbow-measurement.md; per-elbow numbers in the notes above. Shipped in 66cce50 and 0e02225.

title: Make the kitty tab bar read as LCARS chrome
description: The tab bar is the top edge of every lcarcat screen but is currently plain powerline pills. It should read as part of the LCARS frame. Constraint: kitty's tab-bar templates are the only lever — no image protocol is available on that strip.
design:
Used kitty's 'tab_bar_style custom' hook (kitty/tab_bar.py), NOT the title templates.

The bead's own description said templates were the only lever and that no image protocol is available on the strip. The second half is true; the first is wrong. A title template describes ONE tab, so it structurally cannot produce a left rail stub, a right-aligned stardate/clock readout, or any decision that depends on the whole bar. tab_bar_style custom hands draw_tab() every cell of the strip.

The strip is one row, so it obeys one-row LCARS bar rules: flat runs are colored cells, rounded ends are the powerline half-circle glyphs, pills separated by explicit black columns. Tab backgrounds stay black in lcars.conf so the cap glyphs render on black — a cap drawn over a colored bg fills its own rounded notch and squares the corner. The old templates already knew this; the comment explaining it is preserved.

Old templates kept commented in lcars.conf as the documented fallback.

TESTING HAZARD worth remembering: a tab_bar.py that raises takes the tab bar down in EVERY kitty window, including the one being worked in. test/captures/tab_bar.sh therefore builds an isolated KITTY_CONFIG_DIRECTORY from the repo instead of testing via deploy.
close_reason: Custom LCARS tab bar verified across one, two and three tabs — rounded caps flush, colors correct, right-aligned stardate/clock holding position.

title: kitty panes do not share a cell lattice — measured
description:
MEASURED 2026-09-11 against a live kitty (test/screenshot_harness.sh + solid
pane fills + programmatic pixel analysis). Settles an assumption that several
design notes on lcarcat-05h.5 and lcarcat-cg7 were resting on.

QUESTION: in a kitty split, do the panes share one cell grid, or does each
subsection have its own geometry that isn't aligned?

ANSWER: each pane has its OWN grid origin. Adjacent panes are generally NOT
aligned to a common lattice, and the gap between them is a SUB-CELL pixel
quantity that varies continuously with window size.

Vertical split, cell = 19x38 device px, same font both panes:
  os window 1700px -> gap 10px (0.53 cell), pane2 lattice offset  9px  MISALIGNED
  os window 1705px -> gap 15px (0.79 cell), pane2 lattice offset 14px  MISALIGNED
  os window 1710px -> gap 20px (1.05 cell), pane2 lattice offset  0px  aligned
Horizontal (stacked) split, fullscreen:
  pane1 y0..1063 (exactly 28.000 rows), pane2 y1085..2148 (exactly 28.000 rows)
  gap 21px = 0.55 row, lattice offset 21px of a 38px row  MISALIGNED

MECHANISM: kitty gives each pane an integer number of CELLS, then splits the
leftover sub-cell pixels: roughly half into the inter-pane gap (plus the border
width), half to the far edge. Observed gap = leftover//2 + 1 on both axes.
Alignment happens only when that arithmetic lands on a multiple of the cell
size -- a coincidence, not a rule. My first measurement (fullscreen, 181 cols,
gap exactly 19px, phase 0) was exactly that coincidence and nearly led me to
conclude the opposite.

CONSEQUENCES:
 1. Nothing can be aligned ACROSS a kitty pane boundary. The original double
    swoop -- pane A's mirrored elbow meeting pane B's elbow over the divider --
    is not merely expensive, it is UNBUILDABLE in the general case. That is
    likely the real reason it "never fully drew the right-edge stem/fillet"
    (prompt_lcars.zsh:60-67), beyond the ~50ms query and the WINCH trap.
 2. "Make the kitty border one cell of periwinkle" is not expressible. The
    inter-pane space is a variable sub-cell gap plus a border line; a heavy
    periwinkle fill there would be a sliver of changing width.
 3. nvim is the OPPOSITE: it owns one terminal grid, so all its windows share
    one lattice exactly and a separator is exactly 1 cell. The two renderers can
    share a GRAMMAR but never cell-level geometry.
 4. This is a strong argument for the separated-frame grammars (05h.5 D and E):
    each pane frames itself inside its own grid and nothing needs to line up
    across a boundary, so the same rules survive in both renderers. Any grammar
    requiring continuity across a boundary works in nvim and cannot work in
    kitty.

Repro: launch harness, vsplit, `python3 /tmp/lcars_fill.py red|blue` filling each
pane with a solid colour, snapshot, then measure the red/blue bounding boxes and
compare (originB - originA) mod cell_width.

title: Prompt swoop images don't reflow when the pane is resized
description:
User-visible rendering bug. Tracked only as ROADMAP.md prose until now ("Split
resize reflows stale swoop images"); no bead existed. Filed 2026-08-31 with
fresh evidence.

SYMPTOM
A prompt drawn at one pane width, then redrawn after the pane changes width,
leaves its elbow/cap PNGs at the old positions. The bar comes back MANGLED: a
ghost copy of the chip row (elbow + empty chips) stacked directly above the
real text-bearing one, with black notches cut through what should be continuous
periwinkle bar.

REPRODUCED, precisely, 2026-08-28 while shooting README screenshots:
  1. open a kitty window, let the LCARS prompt draw once at full width
  2. vsplit (and/or hsplit) so the pane narrows
  3. the first prompt in scrollback is now visibly broken
Seth spotted it in test/screenshots/rich_demo/05-full-layout.png; visual
inspection confirmed the doubled-bar artifact at the top-left of the left pane
(cols 0-23, rows 0-7): a purple elbow at cols 0-2, a BLANK yellow chip strip
from col 5, a black notch at cols 3-4, black notches at cols 12-13 and 15-17,
and a second text-bearing copy of the same chips ("main", "02-MODIFIED",
"04-UNTRACKED") directly below.

WHY
The flat bar is terminal cells and reflows for free. The elbow and cap are kitty
images. They are placed as Unicode placeholders (U+10EEEE + rowcolumn
diacritics), which was specifically chosen so they scroll and reflow with their
bar — see the comment block above _lc_ph in zsh/prompt_lcars.zsh. That fixed the
"dangling elbow in scrollback" case for SCROLLING. It evidently does not cover
WIDTH changes: on a resize the cells reflow but the image placement does not
follow, so the two disagree.

Worth confirming before designing a fix: is this kitty re-laying-out the
placeholder cells without re-rendering the referenced image grid, or is the
prompt's own reflow arithmetic (fill width, chip drop priority) producing a
different bar for the same scrollback line? _lcars_probe_cell_size /
_lcars_ensure_assets already re-run on WINCH via _LCARS_CELL_DIRTY, so the
asset SIZE is handled; this is about position/layout of already-drawn prompts.

SCOPE NOTE
Only affects prompts already in scrollback. The current prompt redraws correctly
at the new width — that is why this is easy to miss in normal use and why it
only became obvious in a screenshot.

WORKAROUND IN PLACE (not a fix)
test/captures/rich_demo.sh shot 08 clears the pane after the layout is final and
rebuilds the scrollback, so every bar in the README hero was drawn at the width
it is displayed at. Verified all four bars' caps land on the same x. The other
shots (01-07) still carry the artifact and are fine for regression use.

RELATED
lcarcat-qm0.5 is the nvim-side analogue (image invalidation on VimResized), not
this. This one is the zsh/kitty prompt.

Refs: zsh/prompt_lcars.zsh (_lc_ph, _lc_transmit, TRAPWINCH,
_lcars_probe_cell_size), ROADMAP.md "Pending / ideas",
test/captures/rich_demo.sh (shot 08 rationale)
notes:
CORRECTION 2026-08-31 (Seth). My original framing was wrong twice.

1. THIS IS THE WIDTH AXIS, NOT THE CELL-SIZE AXIS.
   Cell pixel size changing (font zoom, display change) is a DIFFERENT problem
   and is already handled: _lcars_probe_cell_size probes via CSI 16t on WINCH
   and _lcars_ensure_assets regenerates a correctly-sized asset set when
   _LCARS_CELL_DIRTY is set. That path works. fvv is about $COLUMNS changing —
   the terminal rewrapping stored lines — with the cell size unchanged.

2. THE SHELL CANNOT FIX THIS, AND THE BEAD SHOULD NOT ASSUME IT CAN.
   zsh and terminal emulators only reflow the CURRENT prompt's line(s). Previous
   prompts are scrollback: the shell does not own them and cannot repaint them.
   So "re-place the images on resize" is not an operation available to
   prompt_lcars.zsh for any bar that has already scrolled. My description above
   implied a fix in that shape; it is not achievable that way.

WHAT THAT LEAVES — reframe before starting.

The bar is two rows of text cells carrying Unicode placeholders (U+10EEEE plus
rowcolumn diacritics). Those were chosen specifically so the image cells live in
the text stream and move with it, which fixed the dangling-elbow-on-SCROLL case.
A width change is different in kind: the two bar rows are independent lines that
rewrap independently, so a rewrap can split or join them and scatter the
placeholder grid — which matches the observed artifact (a blank chip strip above
a text-bearing one, black notches cut through the bar).

Open questions, in the order worth answering:
  a) Is the damage from rewrap of the placeholder cells, or is kitty dropping
     the virtual placement? Distinguish by resizing WIDER vs NARROWER — a pure
     rewrap should be recoverable-looking, a dropped placement should not.
  b) Can it be prevented rather than repaired? A bar that never rewraps cannot
     be scrambled by a rewrap.
  c) Failing that, is the honest outcome "mitigate and document"? Scrollback
     from before a resize being cosmetically wrong is a much smaller problem
     than it looked when I filed this, precisely because it is unfixable from
     the shell and affects only history.

The workaround note still stands: rich_demo.sh shot 08 clears the pane after the
final layout so the README hero contains only bars drawn at their display width.

NOT related to lcarcat-qm0.5 in the way I first claimed — see the correction on
that bead.

title: Cross-language single source of truth: palette, asset naming, shared constants
description:
Flag 2, cross-language half. Four separate things are duplicated across Lua, zsh, Python
and kitty conf, all enforced by hand and by comment.

1. ASSET FILENAME FORMAT — three independent encoders of one structured format:
     generate/gen_swoops.py:93   asset_name()          the generator, source of truth
     nvim/lua/lcars/assets.lua:49 M.asset_name()       hand-maintained Lua mirror
     zsh/prompt_lcars.zsh:37-40                        inline string interpolation,
                                                       not even a function
   gen_swoops.py:110 says "keep this format and the Lua mirror in chrome/assets in sync"
   — and does not mention the zsh consumer at all.

   This is the highest-severity item: a colour mismatch gives a wrong shade, but an
   asset-name mismatch gives a MISSING PNG — silent fallback or broken render.

2. GEOMETRY CONSTANTS crossing the language boundary:
     zsh _LCARS_ELBOW=5 / _LCARS_CAP=2   ==   Lua ELBOW_W=5 / CAP_W=2

3. PALETTE — palette.lua <-> prompt_lcars.zsh:25-34 <-> kitty/lcars.conf:12-37 <->
   colors/lcars.lua (16-colour block). palette.lua:5 states it outright: "Kept in sync
   with those by hand; there is no cross-language import." colors/lcars.lua:19 repeats it
   for the kitty 16-colour set.

4. CELL DIMENSIONS — 19x38 baked into asset filenames, probed independently by zsh
   (CSI 16t, see the csi-16t-cell-size-probe memory) and by Lua (image.nvim
   term.get_size). Related: lcarcat-ul0 (font-geometry epic).

DIRECTION (not decided — needs a call)
Generate the zsh and Lua constant/format files from one source rather than maintaining
mirrors. gen_swoops.py already owns the canonical asset_name(), so it is the natural
generator. Open: whether generated files are committed (simple, no build step at install)
or generated at deploy time (deploy.sh already exists and runs on every change).

Scope this deliberately — it is the piece with the most machinery and the least urgency.
Item 1 alone may be worth doing on its own.

Related: lcarcat-qm0.10 (the within-Lua half), lcarcat-6yz (packaging), lcarcat-ul0.
notes:
UPDATE FROM qm0.9 (2026-08-28) — one new item, one stale line ref, one precedent.

STALE REF: item 1 cites zsh/prompt_lcars.zsh:37-40 for the inline asset-name
interpolation. _lcars_set_asset_paths is now at zsh/prompt_lcars.zsh:46 — it
stayed in the renderer (asset naming is a rendering concern). The prompt is now
two files; the data half, zsh/lcars_prompt_data.zsh, has nothing to do with
assets.

NEW ITEM 5 — CHIP KIND VOCABULARY crosses the language boundary:
    zsh/lcars_prompt_data.zsh  _lcars_build_chips   emits kinds
    nvim/lua/lcars/block_chips.lua  HL table        maps kind -> highlight group
  The set (venv, py, aws, awsdep, git, gitstate, err) is agreed by hand in two
  languages, same as the other four items.

  Severity is LOW, unlike the rest, and the reason is worth copying: block_chips
  has FALLBACK_HL, so an unknown kind renders with default presentation instead
  of vanishing. The failure is a wrong colour, not a missing element.

  Note what is NOT duplicated: the git label WORDS (STAGED/MODIFIED/UNTRACKED,
  zsh/lcars_prompt_data.zsh:75-77) exist only in zsh. nvim treats labels as
  opaque data and never parses them. That asymmetry is deliberate and is the
  pattern the other four items should aim for — send values, not vocabulary.

PRECEDENT WORTH REUSING
qm0.9 solved a narrow version of this bead's problem for the wire protocol, and
the mechanism generalises. Rather than trying to eliminate the duplication, it
made the duplication DETECTABLE: an envelope version that is diagnostic and
never gating, so a mismatched pair warns once and still works
(docs/osc-7447.md "Compatibility"; nvim/lua/lcars/terminal_win.lua
warn_once_on_protocol_skew).

That matters most for item 1. An asset-name mismatch is exactly the failure
class qm0.9 was about: silent, and indistinguishable from working. A generated
manifest checked at load time — or a version stamp on the asset-name format —
would give the same "warn, do not die" property without forcing a single
cross-language importer, which is the expensive fix this bead has been avoiding.

Also relevant: test/unit/run_osc_roundtrip_tests.sh shows how to test a
cross-language contract without merging the implementations — run the real zsh
emitter's output through the real Lua parser and assert they agree. The same
shape would work for asset_name(): generate with gen_swoops.py, resolve with the
Lua and zsh mirrors, assert all three produce the same string.

title: Split prompt_lcars.zsh: headless data/OSC layer shared with the image prompt
description:
>>> SETH HAS A SPECIFIC DIRECTION HERE AND MORE THOUGHTS TO EXPLAIN. Ask him
>>> before designing past this description. The shape below is his steer, not a
>>> proposal to be elaborated independently.

SETH'S DIRECTION (2026-08-27)
Strip the OSC hook out into a separate, headless prompt config — data only, no
rendering, aimed at nvim — and have the full zsh image prompt SHARE that same layer
rather than duplicate it. One source of truth for prompt *data*; kitty graphics
rendering becomes a consumer sitting on top of it, not the thing the data is
entangled with.

WHY (analysis backing the direction)

prompt_lcars.zsh has become a dual-target renderer with a third job bolted on.
_lcars_swoop_precmd branches on _lcars_graphics_ok and either paints kitty graphics
(swoop bar, chip drop-priority, fill arithmetic, placeholder cells) or takes a plain
text fallback — and now, on BOTH paths, also serialises a data feed for a different
consumer entirely.

The dangerous property: the data job has no visual feedback in the environment where
the rendering job runs. If the OSC 7447 payload breaks while you are in kitty, the bar
still looks perfect and nothing tells you. You find out next time you open :LcarsTerm.

Splitting data from rendering fixes that structurally — the headless layer becomes
independently testable (feed it a state, assert on the emitted bytes) without a
terminal, kitty, or screenshots.

RELATED PROBLEMS IN THE SAME AREA (may or may not belong in this bead — ask)

- No version handshake across the boundary. Three protocols cross it: OSC 133
  (standard, borrowed), OSC 7 (standard, borrowed), OSC 7447 (ours, docs/osc-7447.md).
  nvim cannot ask "what do you speak?"; the shell cannot ask "is anyone listening?".

- deploy.sh copies the zsh half to ~/.config/zsh/ and the nvim half to ~/.config/nvim/
  with nothing checking they are the same generation. Not hypothetical: a stale
  ~/.config/nvim/lua/lcars/pty_session.lua silently hijacked the unit suite during the

- The spec's forward-compat rules (unknown kind renders with a default, unknown message
  type ignored, extra fields ignored) cover additive skew only. A grammar change has no
  path.

OPEN QUESTION THIS DECIDES
Is the shell the source of truth for prompt state with nvim as one of several consumers
— in which case the boundary deserves a real contract — or is the shell feed a bridge
until nvim computes this itself? Seth's direction implies the former. Confirm before
investing in protocol machinery.

Refs: docs/osc-7447.md, zsh/prompt_lcars.zsh (_lcars_swoop_precmd, _lcars_emit_chips,
_lcars_graphics_ok), nvim/lua/lcars/pty_session.lua
design:
DECISIONS (Seth, 2026-08-28) — supersedes the earlier hello-message sketch

Correction to my earlier framing: the spec's "no version field, deliberately"
was Seth deferring the work, not a principle to preserve. And its stated
rationale argues against readers GATING on a version, not against the field
existing — I had conflated those.

1. OSC 7447 IS PERMANENT, not a bridge. py/git/gitstate are derivable by nvim
   from the OSC 7 cwd alone; venv ($VIRTUAL_ENV) and aws/awsdep ($AWS_PROFILE)
   are the live env of a process nvim spawned and cannot inspect (no /proc on
   macOS; `ps eww` prints argv without environ — verified). Once the channel
   exists for those two, carrying git/py over it is free and spares nvim a
   duplicate `git status --porcelain` per prompt. `err` stays nvim-computed
   from OSC 133;D via block_chips.outcome.

2. VERSION LIVES IN THE ENVELOPE, NO HELLO MESSAGE.
     ESC ] 7447 ; lcars ; <version> ; <message> [ ; <field> ]... ST
   Rejected: a one-shot `hello` at pty open. It fires once per shell process
   (plus on re-source, which deploy.sh:104 instructs), and nvim's on_stdout is
   wired by jobstart before the shell writes — so no race in the :LcarsTerm
   case. But it is a one-shot ANNOUNCEMENT: any consumer not listening at that
   instant never learns the version and cannot ask. That bites on mid-session
   nvim lua reload, on attaching to an already-running kitty shell, and for any
   consumer that did not spawn the shell. An envelope version rides every
   prompt instead — stateless, nothing to miss, ~5 bytes.
   Rejected: a TRAILING version field on `chips`. Old parsers pair fields two
   at a time from after `chips`, so a trailing field is detected only by odd
   field count (fragile), and a LEADING one would make an old parser read the
   version as a kind and the first real kind as its label — silent garbage,
   the exact misparse the spec forbids.
   Placing the version BEFORE the message type makes this a clean break: the
   existing `^7447;lcars;chips;(.*)$` match simply fails, so old readers ignore
   rather than misparse. It is also the LAST breaking change — from here every
   change negotiates.
   Reverse direction ("is anyone listening?") needs no pty traffic: nvim sets
   LCARS_TERM_PROTO=<ver> via jobstart's `env` opt (pty_session.lua:262).

3. SKEW RESPONSE: warn once per session via vim.notify naming both versions and
   pointing at deploy.sh, then render best-effort anyway. Closes the ba0 failure
   mode (a stale nvim showing no chips was indistinguishable from a shell
   emitting none) without making a skewed deploy unusable.

4. LAYER SCOPE: emission + hook installation. The headless layer sets NO PROMPT.
   The plain-text fallback PROMPT stays in prompt_lcars.zsh as its degraded
   render path.

5. DOC SCOPE (my call, not asked): document the new envelope and rewrite
   Compatibility; leave the four Open Questions open and the doc experimental.

HOOK ORDERING (what makes this more than a file move)
_lcars_swoop_precmd enforces one order inside a single function: 133;D first
(before any decorative output) -> cell probe -> gather -> render bar -> A,
chips, OSC 7, B last. Render must interleave BETWEEN the data layer's halves.
Data layer exposes an install taking the render hooks as args, yielding
precmd_functions [data_open, render, data_close] and preexec [render, data_C],
so ordering is stated in one place rather than by array-index surgery.

title: chrome phase 5: general pane-edge split model (VISUAL REVIEW REQUIRED)
description:
>>> SETH WANTS TO VISUALLY REVIEW THE PROPOSED CHANGES BEFORE THEY LAND. <<<
>>> He expects to agree, but wants to see mockups/screenshots first. Do NOT
>>> ship this phase on the strength of the description alone — build the
>>> mockup, show it, get the nod, then implement.

This is the only phase that changes what the screen looks like.

CURRENT MODEL — "outer frame only" (chrome.lua:156): one top-left corner, one bottom-left
corner, interior edges get capped channels. It degrades past a single split:

- frame_panes only runs for a.row == top_row and for the bottom row, so A PANE IN THE
  MIDDLE OF A 3-WAY VERTICAL STACK GETS NO CORNER TREATMENT AT ALL.
- The horizontal-separator loop breaks after the first matching window below (line 221),
  emitting one separator segment per upper window regardless of how many panes sit beneath.
- lx = (c0 == 0) and rail_width or c0 special-cases the screen's left edge, so interior and
  edge separators follow different rules.
- far_right_cap applies only to the last window in a row, leaving a middle column's right
  edge uncapped.

DESIGN-LANGUAGE INCONSISTENCY: kitty and nvim disagree about what a split looks like.
kitty (_LCARS_SPLIT_SWOOP / _lcars_detect_pane in prompt_lcars.zsh) is per-pane — an elbow
on every side that abuts another pane. nvim is one global outer frame. Same concept, two
philosophies, so a kitty split and an nvim split do not look like the same system.

PROPOSAL: adopt kitty's rule in nvim, because it is the one that generalises. Model the
screen as a set of PANE EDGES and give every edge a terminator determined only by what it
abuts:

  screen edge        -> elbow into the rail
  neighbouring pane  -> capped channel + 1-col gap
  tabline/statusline -> elbow into that bar

No special cases for "top row" or "left edge", no global outer-frame concept. A 2x2 grid
then works for the same reason a single split does, and nvim matches kitty.

Depends on phase 4: the pure plan.lua is what makes it possible to assert the edge grammar
across many topologies without screenshotting each one.
design:
PREMISE CHECK (2026-09-01), read before designing.

This bead says 'adopt kitty's rule in nvim, because it is the one that
generalises'. Kitty's rule is real but it is NOT what kitty currently does:
_LCARS_SPLIT_SWOOP in zsh/prompt_lcars.zsh:68 is empty, i.e. DISABLED, and has
been. With it off the bar is always left-elbow + right-cap, exactly like nvim's
outer frame. So:

 - Do not compare a live nvim split against a live kitty split and expect to see
   the two design languages disagree. You will see the same thing twice. Set
   _LCARS_SPLIT_SWOOP=1 first if you want the per-pane version on screen.
 - The stated reasons for disabling it (prompt_lcars.zsh:60-67) are mostly
   costs that DO NOT transfer to nvim: a ~50ms 'kitty @ ls' neighbour query per
   prompt, and a SIGWINCH trap to invalidate it. chrome.lua already has full
   window topology in-process for free, so the expensive part of kitty's rule is
   free on the nvim side. That strengthens the proposal rather than weakening it.
 - The one reason that DOES transfer is 'the right-edge stem/fillet it never
   fully drew'. A per-pane grammar needs a terminator for every edge including
   the right one, and that is the specific piece that defeated the kitty
   implementation. Design it explicitly; do not assume the mirrored elbow asset
   is sufficient.

Assets: mirrored elbow-top-right and cap-round-left already exist and are
generated by gen_swoops.py — they are used ONLY by the disabled split-swoop
path (prompt_lcars.zsh:38-39), so the art for a per-pane grammar is largely
already there.
notes:
REV 4 (2026-09-11). Generator REBUILT and now lives in the repo at
generate/mockup_edges.py -- the rev-1..3 copy lived in a session scratchpad and
was cleaned up between sessions, which is why it is in-tree now. Regenerate with
  python3 generate/mockup_edges.py /tmp/lcars-mockup/edge-grammar.html
It self-verifies on build and REFUSES to emit the page if any grammar produces a
same-cell collision or an out-of-bounds placement. Current: 207 placements,
A=42 B=48 C=42 D=33 E=42, zero problems.

Artifact updated in place (same URL):
https://claude.ai/code/artifact/16ca7190-3938-4ddd-a6aa-a68ec94e5818

TWO MEASUREMENTS CHANGED THE ANSWER SINCE REV 3:

1. E IS CHEAPER THAN I COSTED IT. I said two text rows per pane; it is ONE.
   Swapping laststatus=3 for per-window statuslines is ROW-NEUTRAL -- the
   statuslines replace the separator rows and the global bar already being
   spent. Headless nvim, 3 stacked windows in 28 lines:
     laststatus=3 winbar off -> 23 text rows
     laststatus=2 winbar off -> 23 text rows   (the swap is free)
     laststatus=2 winbar on  -> 20 text rows   (winbar = exactly 1/pane)
   So C, D and E all cost the same one winbar row per pane. E returns a complete
   three-sided frame for it, which makes E strictly the best of the three on
   budget. E's only real cost is BEHAVIOURAL: every pane shows its own
   statusline instead of one global bar showing the focused window's info.
   lualine's inactive_sections (statusline.lua:88) already covers the styling.

2. KITTY PANES DO NOT SHARE A CELL LATTICE (lcarcat-qbg). This kills the
   "nvim and kitty splits become the same object at cell level" premise that
   grammar B rested on, and it kills the mirrored-elbow double swoop outright --
   unbuildable, not merely expensive. It also argues FOR D and E specifically:
   each pane frames itself inside its own grid and nothing needs to line up
   across a boundary, so those rules are the only ones that survive in both
   renderers.

RECOMMENDATION UNCHANGED BUT NOW BETTER SUPPORTED: E.

OPEN: (1) D or E; (2) which square corner -- right angle both sides (free, drawn)
vs rounded outer + squared inner (a new gen_swoops variant; elbow(fillet=False)
already renders it); (3) are per-pane statuslines acceptable.

title: chrome phase 4: split compute_placements into topology -> plan -> assets
description:
compute_placements() (chrome.lua:138-310) is ~170 lines mixing five concerns: window
discovery, policy (tabline_visible, the terminal-buffer suppression), topology reasoning,
asset filename construction, and coordinate math. It reads vim state throughout, so it can
only be tested by launching a real nvim and taking a picture.

  chrome/topology.lua   vim windows -> pure layout model { panes, edges, corners }
  chrome/plan.lua       layout model + policy -> placements   (PURE, testable)
  chrome/assets.lua     placement -> asset name/path (mostly exists in assets.lua)
  chrome.lua            lifecycle, policy flags, registry registration

The win is plan.lua as a pure function: feed it a synthetic 2x2 grid, a 3-way vertical
stack, nested splits, and assert on the placement list. That is the ONLY practical way to
attack the multi-split problem in phase 5 — screenshotting every split topology does not
scale, and screenshots are exactly what let the current breakage go unnoticed.

Prerequisite for phase 5. Pure refactor, no visual change.

title: chrome phase 2: registry owns invalidation via layer dirty-specs
description:
The separator bug was a missing WinScrolled subscription. Adding the event (7701abc) is a
patch — the next component that places an image will make the same mistake, because the
rule currently exists only as a paragraph in docs/nvim-chrome.md.

Structural version: layers declare when they go dirty, and the registry runs ONE debounced
reconcile pass for all of them.

  registry.register_layer("chrome", {
    events   = { "VimResized", "WinResized", "WinNew", "WinClosed",
                 "TabEnter", "BufWinEnter", "WinEnter" },
    volatile = true,
    plan     = chrome.compute_placements,
  })

`volatile = true` is the point: "re-place me whenever ANY layer reconciles". That is exactly
the prose rule — a component placing kitty images must re-place on events that cause a
NEIGHBOUR to redraw, not only on events that change its own geometry. chrome sets it because
its images sit on rows the frame layer scrolls through; the frame layer does not need it.

Turns "remember to subscribe to your neighbour's events" from tribal knowledge into a
declaration. Keep the existing 80ms debounce semantics (chrome.lua:395-404).

title: chrome phase 1: registry becomes the only caller of image.nvim
description:
Make image_registry.lua actually be what its header already claims to be.

Blocker to fix first: registry.place() hardcodes `window = win, buffer = buf` plus a
render_offset_top = -1 workaround. chrome needs WINDOWLESS absolute-screen placement (see
chrome.lua's "+1 float trap" note) and cannot use it as written.

1. Two placement addresses, exactly one per placement:
     { win = w, buf = b, row = r, col = c }   buffer-bound, scrolls with content
     { screen_x = x, screen_y = y }           windowless, absolute cell

2. Declarative reconcile instead of imperative place/clear:
     registry.reconcile(layer, placements)
   `layer` is an owner tag ("chrome", "frame", "eob"). `placements` is the COMPLETE desired
   set for that layer; the registry diffs against the previous plan, clears what is gone,
   creates what is new, leaves unchanged handles alone. This is chrome.lua's render_all
   (329-358) generalised, so every layer gets the dedupe-by-key behaviour only chrome has.

Deletes: chrome.state.imgs, chrome.placement_key, chrome.clear_all, chrome.render_all.
Then (can be a follow-up) block_demo.tab_imgs and terminal_frame's inline table.

Pure refactor — no visual change. Verify with test/integration/terminal_win.sh plus the
separator pixel-diff check from the ba0 session.
notes:
MERGED FROM lcarcat-qm0.6 (filed 2026-08-20, superseded by this bead 2026-08-27).

qm0.6 asked for the same migration. Content folded in:
 - Preserve the selective stale-key clearing pattern (clear placements no longer in the
   new set, keep unchanged ones) — that is what reconcile() formalises.
 - chrome.lua's generate-on-miss via jobstart STAYS until lcarcat-qm0.4 (generate-on-miss
   in the registry) lands, then it can be removed from chrome too.
 - qm0.6's precondition — 'do this after frame_renderer has used image_registry in
   production, to prove the API is right' — is now SATISFIED: frame_renderer and
   terminal_win both use it as of the ba0 work.

What this bead adds over qm0.6: qm0.6 assumed chrome could just call registry.place().
It cannot — place() hardcodes window/buffer binding plus render_offset_top=-1, and chrome
needs windowless absolute-screen placement. Extending the registry with two placement
addresses is a PREREQUISITE, not a detail.

DESIGN INPUT (2026-09-01, see lcarcat-dat): nvim 0.13 ships vim.ui.img, an experimental
built-in kitty-graphics API that is almost exactly this bead's WINDOWLESS address —
absolute screen cells, flicker-free relocation of an existing placement, and a per-image
z-index that image.nvim does not expose. It is unusable today (Seth's nvim is 0.12.2) and
dat is blocked on that, but shape the windowless address so it could dispatch to a
different backend later rather than hardcoding image.nvim behind it. Keep the dedupe cache
in OUR layer either way: vim.ui.img re-transmits the bytes on every placement, and lcarcat
places the same few elbow/cap PNGs repeatedly.

title: (EPIC) chrome.lua image handling: one owner, testable plan, general split model
description:
chrome.lua predates the shared image/render library work and never joined it. Three
problems, in increasing order of how much design judgement they need.

1. FOUR image owners, not one. image_registry.lua's own header claims "frame_renderer,
   terminal_frame, and chrome all share a single ownership model" — that is aspirational.
   Only frame_renderer and terminal_win use it. chrome.lua:349, block_demo.lua:109 and
   terminal_frame.lua:65 each call image.from_file directly against private handle tables.
   chrome *cannot* adopt the registry as written: registry.place() hardcodes
   window/buffer binding, while chrome needs windowless absolute-screen placement.

2. The plan is untestable. compute_placements() (chrome.lua:138-310) is ~170 lines mixing
   window discovery, policy, topology reasoning, asset naming and coordinate math, reading
   vim state throughout. It can only be exercised by launching nvim and taking a picture,
   which is why multi-split breakage went unnoticed.

3. The split model is "outer frame only" and does not generalise past one split. Separately,
   nvim ("one outer frame") and kitty ("elbow on every side that abuts a pane",
   _LCARS_SPLIT_SWOOP in prompt_lcars.zsh) use different design languages for the same idea.

Motivating incident: the display/input separator losing its ends on scroll (fixed in
7701abc by adding WinScrolled to chrome's autocmd list). That was not a logic error — it
was two components writing the same screen row with no arbitration, invisible to every
state-dump assertion, surviving redraw!, and self-healing on WinEnter so it read as
flakiness. The fix was a patch; phases 1-3 are the structural version.

Phases 1-2 are pure refactor, no visual change. Phase 3 is small once 1 lands. Phase 4
unblocks 5. Phase 5 is the only one that changes what you see.

title: Regression test: chrome images cleared by a neighbour's scroll
description:
The separator-row bug (chrome elbow/cap images on the display/input separator going black after scrolling, fixed by adding WinScrolled to chrome.lua's autocmd list) is invisible to every existing assertion — it lives entirely in the kitty image layer, survives redraw!, and self-heals on WinEnter, so it cannot be caught by frame_buffer state dumps.

A working repro exists (developed in the lcarcat-ba0 session): open :LcarsTerm, run several commands to make the display scrollable, wincmd k, C-u x4, screenshot, then measure the separator row.

The assertion that worked: derive the separator's screen row from nvim window geometry (win_screenpos + height) rather than eyeballing, then pixel-diff that row's band against the pre-scroll capture. Identical = pass. Before the fix it was 10874/131328 px different; after, 0.

Turn that into test/integration/chrome_scroll_separator.sh. The geometry-derived-row + pixel-diff-against-baseline technique generalizes to any 'image layer got clobbered' bug and is worth having as a reusable helper.
notes:
WORKING REPRO NOW IN THE REPO (2026-08-27): test/integration/chrome_scroll_separator_repro.sh

It reproduces, derives the separator row from nvim's own window geometry, derives cell
height from the capture, and prints the pixel-diff. Verified end-to-end against the fixed
build: separator cell row 50, cell height 38px, 0/131328 px differ on both B-scrolled and
C-after-redraw.

Remaining work for this bead is small: turn the printed measurement into a pass/fail exit
code, and confirm it FAILS on a build with the WinScrolled subscription removed from
chrome.lua (that is the part that proves the test has teeth — it was 10874/131328 px
before the fix). Then rename off the _repro suffix.

The harness also deliberately captures C-after-redraw: if the separator does not return
after redraw!, the damage is in the image layer rather than the highlight layer. Keep that
step, it is the diagnostic.

title: term_input: set filetype to zsh/bash to match the running shell
description:
term_input.lua's input buffer has no filetype set. terminal_win.lua spawns the PTY with vim.env.SHELL or '/bin/zsh' (terminal_win.lua ~line 193), so the input buffer's content is shell syntax matching whatever that resolves to -- but there's no syntax highlighting for it since filetype is unset.

Set the input buffer's filetype from the same shell_cmd used to start the PTY: derive the basename (zsh/bash/etc), map to the matching nvim filetype ('zsh' or 'bash'; fall back to 'sh' for anything else), and set it via vim.bo[buf].filetype in term_input.lua's M.open() (or have terminal_win.lua pass it through opts, matching how it already passes win/on_submit/min_height/max_height).
acceptance_criteria: Typing a shell command in the term_input buffer shows shell syntax highlighting (strings, comments, $VARS) matching the actual shell (zsh vs bash), not plain text.
notes: Implemented: terminal_win.lua now derives shell_cmd once (vim.env.SHELL or /bin/zsh), computes its basename, and passes filetype='zsh'|'bash'|'sh' through term_input.open()'s opts (mirroring how win/on_submit/min_height/max_height are already threaded). term_input.lua sets vim.bo[buf].filetype = opts.filetype when provided -- optional, so existing callers/tests that don't pass it are unaffected. Both files syntax-checked clean via nvim --headless loadfile().

title: terminal-win: PTY width should be the frame's content width, not the raw window width
description:
Found while manually testing :LcarsTerm (lcarcat-2z9): `ls` output runs off
the right edge of the window.

Root cause: terminal_win.lua's M.open() sizes the PTY from the raw display
window width —

  local width = vim.api.nvim_win_get_width(display_win)
  pty_session.start(shell, { width = width, height = height }, callbacks)

— but that's not the width actually visible inside the frame. Two things
eat into it that this calculation ignores:

1. frame_buffer's own bar width (bw) is computed as
   `vim.api.nvim_win_get_width(display_win) - 14` (reserves margin for the
   header/footer's elbow+cap images) — terminal_win.lua already does this
   subtraction for bw, but never applies anything equivalent to the PTY
   width it passes to pty_session.start().
2. Content lines get an additional left indent before any real text:
   frame_renderer.render_content() writes `pad(lp) .. " " .. l` (lp=6, so
   real content starts at column 7).

Tools like `ls` query the PTY's reported width (COLUMNS / ioctl TIOCGWINSZ)
to size their multi-column output — with the current (too-wide) value, `ls`
formats assuming more horizontal room than the frame's content area
actually has, and the display window has wrap=false, so the overflow is
clipped invisibly off the right edge rather than wrapping.

Fix direction: PTY width should be based on the frame's actual content
width, roughly `window_width - lp - 1` for the left margin — verify
empirically against a real wide-output command (`ls`, `ls -la` in a big
directory) whether the right side should also stay within bw's boundary
for visual consistency with the header/footer bar, rather than assuming
the formula without checking. Height wasn't reported as an issue but is
worth a quick sanity check too, since it's computed the same
unadjusted way.

title: terminal frame images don't scroll/hide with the display buffer
description:
image_registry.place() uses image.nvim's absolute x/y floating placement,
not scroll-following Unicode placeholders — contradicts the design doc's
"Why Unicode placeholder images, not absolute placement" section. Images
are positioned once at placement time using the window's topline; never
repositioned afterward.

Discovered while manually testing :LcarsTerm (lcarcat-2z9).

Symptoms:
- Switching buffers in the display window leaves old elbow/cap images
  floating over whatever buffer is now shown there.
- Manually scrolling the display window (e.g. zt) leaves images pinned
  at their original screen row while the text scrolls underneath them.
- Compounds with terminal_win.lua's scroll-to-bottom-on-output behavior
  (added in 2z9): more frequent scrolling makes the detached-image
  artifact show up more often, not less.

Fix direction: chrome.lua already solves this exact problem for its own
images via clear_all()+render_all() wired to WinScrolled/BufWinEnter/
WinEnter/WinResized/etc (see chrome.lua:428-441). Add a
frame_buffer.reposition_images() that iterates M.blocks and re-places
each block's images at the current window scroll offset (clearing stale
image keys first via renderer.clear_images), then wire terminal_win.lua's
display window to the same autocmd set, calling reposition_images() and
clearing images on BufLeave/WinLeave from the display buffer.
notes:
Follow-up from user's manual test (fresh nvim instance):

1. VERTICAL OFFSET (fixed): header/footer bg bars were 1 row higher than the elbow/cap images. Root-caused to an off-by-one in the installed image.nvim (3rd/image.nvim @ 5c6f29a, 2026-08-19): renderer.lua's window+buffer-bound 'on topline' branch (~line 266, absolute_y = win_info.winrow) and its normal fully-visible branch (~line 344, absolute_y = screen_pos.row) both assign a 1-indexed getwininfo/screenpos row straight into absolute_y without the -1 the kitty backend expects (backends/kitty/init.lua:154 does write_graphics_at(cfg, x+1, y+1), confirming 0-indexed input). image.nvim's own partial-scroll branch (line 324) already has an explicit -1 and wasn't affected. Worked around in nvim/lua/lcars/image_registry.lua by passing render_offset_top = -1 to image.from_file() -- that option is added to absolute_y in exactly the two buggy branches and explicitly skipped during real partial-scroll clipping (renderer.lua:348), so it's a scoped correction, not a blind offset. Did not touch input y (buf_row) directly since that also feeds topline/botline branch-selection comparisons and would have desynced those instead.

2. HORIZONTAL SCROLL (mitigated, not fixed): user confirmed images don't track horizontal scroll and okayed just disabling it for now (separate bead already covers output-width handling for the actual long-line root cause). Added a WinScrolled autocmd in terminal_win.lua's M.open() scoped to display_win that snaps leftcol back to 0 via winrestview whenever it drifts -- self-limiting (no leftcol change -> no further event). Vertical scrolling untouched.

Changed further: nvim/lua/lcars/image_registry.lua (render_offset_top=-1 in M.place's image.from_file() opts), nvim/lua/lcars/terminal_win.lua (WinScrolled leftcol-pin autocmd in M.open()).

Still needs the human capture-test pass from the first note (frame_renderer.sh/frame_buffer.sh + scroll-back-to-top + buffer-switch) -- please re-check vertical alignment specifically now that render_offset_top is in place, and confirm horizontal scroll no longer drags images. Still IN_PROGRESS, not committed.
close_reason: Fixed: switched to image.nvim window+buffer-bound placement, corrected upstream off-by-one via render_offset_top=-1, pinned horizontal scroll. User confirmed visually in a fresh nvim instance.

title: term-input: theme gutter-EOB-fill backfill + elbow/header/footer chrome
description:
term_input.lua's orange styling is incomplete, and it has no framing chrome
at all. Feedback from Seth after reviewing the merged lyz implementation:

1. The input panel's "stem" has TWO areas that both need to be orange:
   - The built-in gutter (LineNr/SignColumn cells, where ruler lines
     appear) — this IS orange already, via term_input.open()'s winhighlight
     (LineNr/SignColumn -> LcarsTermInputStem).
   - The gutter-EOB-fill backfill (nvim/lua/lcars/gutter_eob_fill.lua) —
     fills the area between the end of the gutter and the end of the
     window on below-end-of-buffer rows, via a style="minimal" floating
     window. This is currently periwinkle, not orange, because its float
     hardcodes winhighlight = "Normal:SignColumn,NormalNC:SignColumn,
     EndOfBuffer:SignColumn" — it resolves the GLOBAL "SignColumn"
     highlight group by name, not through whatever window-local
     winhighlight remapping the window it's filling for has set up. It has
     no concept of a per-window override today.

2. Overall framing: the elbow images, header bar, and footer bar around
   the input panel should be periwinkle (the standard LCARS frame color —
   matching frame_buffer's display window chrome) — orange is reserved for
   the stem alone, to mark "this is the input panel." term_input.lua
   currently has zero framing chrome (no elbows, no header/footer bars) —
   it's a bare highlighted split.

## Likely approach (needs design review before implementing)

- gutter_eob_fill.lua needs some notion of a per-window highlight-group
  override (e.g. a registration table window id -> override group name)
  so its float can resolve to LcarsTermInputStem instead of the global
  SignColumn, OR term_input.lua manages its own EOB fill independently of
  the generic global mechanism. Trade-off between a shared mechanism vs.
  input-panel-specific code needs a decision.
- Header/footer/elbow chrome: reuse the pattern in
  nvim/lua/lcars/frame_renderer.lua (render_header, render_footer,
  place_images, elbow_path/felbow_path) and image_registry.lua's PNG
  transmit/cache, adapted for a much shorter panel (term_input is a
  handful of rows, not a scrolling block history).

## Do not implement without design sign-off

Seth wants to review design changes to the input panel's top and bottom
bars before implementation — this is explicitly NOT a "figure it out and
build it" task. Raise the design questions (chrome layout for a short
fixed-height panel, whether/how it echoes frame_buffer's header/footer
shape) before writing code.

title: terminal-frame: resize detection + image invalidation on VimResized
description:
Wire up font/window resize detection in terminal_frame.lua so that image
assets are invalidated and regenerated when cell pixel dimensions change.

On VimResized autocmd (already registered in M.setup()):
  1. Re-probe cell dims via assets.cell_px() (CSI 16t query)
  2. Compare against image_registry's stored current_cw/current_ch
  3. If changed: call image_registry.M.reset(), then M.refresh()
     — refresh() will call get_id() which generates missing assets on cache miss

This makes font zoom (ctrl+shift+= / ctrl+shift+-) and display changes
seamless: the next refresh picks up the new dims, regenerates PNGs if needed,
and retransmits at the correct pixel size.

Failure handling: CSI 16t probe can time out on non-kitty terminals — keep
the existing dims and skip invalidation rather than clearing a working cache.

Depends on lcarcat-qm0.4 (generate-on-miss) — resize detection is only useful
once get_id() can generate missing assets.
notes:
pty_session.resize(width, height) now exists (added for lcarcat-biv) — jobresize wrapper. The VimResized handler can call it directly with geometry(win)'s content_width and the new window height; no new primitive needed on the PTY side.

Third case to handle, also from biv: while alternate-screen passthrough is
active the frame is not what the PTY is drawing into — a full-screen program
is drawing into alternate_screen's float. terminal_win resizes the PTY on
entering and leaving passthrough, but nothing resizes it if the user resizes
nvim (or the OS window) WHILE a program is up, so vim/htop keep the size they
were handed and draw to a screen that is no longer there. VimResized must
branch: alternate_screen.active() -> resize to alternate_screen.size(),
otherwise -> resize to the frame's content_width/height.

title: Per-row image placement for progressive viewport clipping
description:
image.nvim hides an image entirely when its buffer anchor row scrolls above the viewport topline — there is no partial clipping. For LCARS elbow/hcap chrome, this means the full 3-row elbow disappears as soon as row 0 scrolls off, rather than showing rows 1-2 while row 0 is hidden.

Fix: place one image.nvim from_file() per elbow row instead of one image for the full elbow. A 3-row elbow becomes three 5x1 placements, each anchored to its own buffer row (y=0, y=1, y=2). As the buffer scrolls, row 0 disappears first, then row 1, then row 2 — clean progressive clipping with no custom math.

image_registry.lua should expose a place_image(buf, win, path, row, col, w) call that issues one placement per source row. frame_renderer.lua calls it once per elbow/hcap row when building the header/footer.

Acceptance:
